 Guest Commentary: A lack of funding for SNAP threatens military readiness

 By Mark Hertling PUBLISHED: October 31, 2026 at 5:30 AM EDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... $900 million. That is the staggering sum Florida lawmakers must find in the state budget for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) next year, or we could soon face a surge in childhood hunger. As a former soldier who spent nearly four decades in uniform, and one who understands how the health of our nation’s youth is critically important to national security, I look at this looming shortfall not just as a fiscal crisis, but as a direct threat to the strength of our nation.
 In 2009, I was appointed as the Army’s Deputy Commanding General of Initial Military Training (IMT), the Army’s “basic training.” I had the responsibility to oversee the training of 160,000 incoming recruits annually. Tasked by my commander to provide an assessment of the young men and women arriving at basic training, I was surprised to find the majority of them were physically underprepared for the training required for their future military service. The root causes? Poor nutrition and a lack of adequate physical preparation. We had 10 weeks to get them in physical shape, as well as train them in the skills of soldiering.  Not surprisingly, the challenges facing our armed forces — and our nation’s youth — continue to increase since my time in command, as the U.S. Department of Defense data reports that 77% of young Americans ages 17 to 24 are ineligible for military service, primarily due to their fitness level.
 The increasing low levels of physical readiness are a result of many societal issues, but poor nutrition and a lack of proper physical activity in schools and at home are the central issue. Especially important, what children eat depends on what their families can afford, and nearly one in five households experience food insecurity. When a family cannot afford nutritious food, health suffers.
 To fuel the next generation of military personnel, we must rely on our nation’s most effective, existing frontline defenses against hunger. SNAP is one of those. Leaders in Florida have recognized the link between food assistance and wellness, taking steps to restrict SNAP purchases of items like candy and soda and direct aid toward more nourishing options. But nutrition guidelines cannot succeed if families lack access to SNAP benefits, and a recent policy change puts that access at risk.
 Previously, the federal government covered the entirety of SNAP benefits while splitting administrative costs 50/50 with states. When Congress passed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, it overhauled the historic state-federal funding partnership. Under the new law, states must now cover 75% of administrative costs and, for the first time, assume financial liability for a portion of benefit funding based on state-level administration.
 Congress granted a two-year transition period to give states more time to upgrade their technology and SNAP administrative systems. But the additional two-year grace period currently only applies to a handful of states. Florida is not one of those, as we are on the hook to pay next year.
 Without an adjustment from Congress to grant all states the additional time to update their systems to the new law, Florida is staring down a $900 million mandate. The financial strain on the state could jeopardize the program, leaving thousands of children in Florida without the basic nutrition required to grow into healthy adults. Since Florida has historically had one of the highest rates of representation in the U.S. military, the health of our youth is key to national security.
 In the military, we train to prevent injuries before they happen. Allowing SNAP to falter in Florida would be an unforced injury to our families and our long-term national security. Congress must treat all states equally, and extend the grace period already granted to a few states. We cannot successfully defend our nation tomorrow if we fail to feed our children well today.
 Mark Hertling of Orlando is a retired U.S. Army Lieutenant General with 38 years of service. Since retiring from the military, he has served as a healthcare executive, national security analyst and commentator, and teaches leadership.
